summary: Reports the experience of one MIT group that implemented both the user and server sides of the new Telnet protocol. It discusses the Go-Ahead mechanism and gives suggestions for a smoother changeover, since the new Telnet is not compatible with the old one.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 559 records MIT's experience implementing a new version of Telnet and explains why Go Ahead signals were difficult to send reliably. It recommends suppressing those signals by default to ease compatibility, while retaining a way to request them.

questions: what is go ahead in telnet
why was go ahead difficult to implement
subtitle: Implementation lessons from MIT's new Telnet user and server programs.

tldr.problem: MIT found that the new Telnet protocol was not compatible with the old one, and its server could not reliably tell when a user's process was waiting for input to send Go Ahead.
tldr.mechanism: The report describes MIT's handling of Telnet options and control sequences, an idle-time approach to sending Go Ahead, and separate server sockets for experimentation and compatibility.
tldr.outcome: The author recommends making Suppress Go Ahead the default while allowing hosts that need Go Ahead to request it.

today: RFC 559 is a historical implementation report about an early Telnet protocol transition and the problems MIT encountered.

sections.title: Two Telnet Versions
sections.content:
MIT-DN implemented both user and server programs for the new Telnet protocol. The new protocol was not compatible with the old one, so the transition caused problems when MIT briefly tried the new programs and many hosts did not recognize the new control sequences.

The server implemented ECHO and Suppress Go Ahead options and recognized several control sequences, including Interrupt Process, Erase Character, Abort Output, Are You There, Break and Synch.
sections.plainLanguage: MIT built both ends of the new Telnet protocol, but older hosts did not understand its control signals. The report shares implementation details to help other sites make the transition.

sections.title: Handling Go Ahead and Control Signals
sections.content:
The server could not reliably know when a user's process was waiting for network input. MIT's workaround was to wait 2.5 seconds after sending output; if no more output appeared, the server sent Go Ahead and waited for input or output. This usually worked but could send an extra signal, and the report does not claim it was reliable in every case.

The report also describes how the server translated control signals into local terminal actions. For example, Interrupt Process used the system interrupt character, while handling of Abort Output depended on the receiving program.
sections.plainLanguage: The server could not see reliably when a user was ready to type, so it guessed after a period without output. That guess usually worked, but sometimes produced an extra Go Ahead signal.

sections.title: Testing the New Protocol and Suppressing Go Ahead
sections.content:
MIT kept a compatibility server on socket 1 that did not begin option negotiation and did not send Go Ahead unless requested. It also proposed an experimental server on socket 60 (octal 105) that followed the new protocol and invited other hosts to test their clients against it.

The author argues that Suppress Go Ahead should be the default because only a few hosts named in the report required Go Ahead. Hosts that need the signal could still negotiate to receive it.
sections.plainLanguage: MIT kept a server for older clients and offered a separate socket for testing the new protocol. The author recommends that servers stay quiet by default and send Go Ahead only when a host requests it.
